extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, astronomers, mathematicians, and readers of Newton's Principia
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Newton's hypotheses, theorems, propositions and corollaries about gravitation and planetary motion (Latin text of Principia). Contains theoretical claims, experimental remarks, numerical estimates and problems for computing orbital elements and comparative weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. VIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas primarios radiis ad Terram ductis areas describere temporibus minimè proportionales; at radiis ad Solem ductis areas temporibus proportionales percurrere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that with respect to the Earth planets sometimes advance, stand still or retrograde, while with respect to the Sun they always advance and describe areas proportional to times — an astronomical proposition demonstrated especially from the eclipses of Jupiter's satellites (given as empirical support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypoth. IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam radio ad centrum terræ ducto aream tempori proportionalem describere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts the Moon describes areas proportional to times with radius drawn to Earth's center; remark that lunar motion is slightly perturbed by the Sun but such minute errors are neglected for these hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I. Theor. I
rubrics_metrics.description: Vires, quibus Planetæ circumjoviales perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis & in orbibus suis retinentur, respicere centrum Jovis, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum locorum ab eodem centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that the forces causing the moons of Jupiter to be retained in their orbits act toward Jupiter and are inversely proportional to the square of the distance from Jupiter; prior parts are justified by earlier hypotheses and propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II. Theor. II
rubrics_metrics.description: Vires, quibus Planetæ primarii perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis, & in Orbibus suis retinentur, respicere Solem, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that the forces keeping the primary planets in their orbits are directed to the Sun and vary inversely as the squares of the distances; supported by Hypothesis VIII and earlier propositions and discussed via the smallness of apse motion if the inverse-square law held.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III. Theor. III
rubrics_metrics.description: Vim qua Luna retinetur in Orbe suo respicere terram, & esse reciprocò ut quadratum distantiæ locorum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims the force that retains the Moon in its orbit is directed to the Earth and inversely proportional to the square of the distance; argument includes estimates of lunar apogee motion and small corrections due to solar action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV. Theor. IV
rubrics_metrics.description: Lunam gravitare in terram, & vi gravitatis retrahi semper à motu rectilineo, & in orbe suo retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates (with numerical estimates and pendulum/fall experiments) that the force retaining the Moon in orbit is the same gravity experienced on Earth's surface; calculation compares distances, times and observed free-fall distances and assumes Earth at rest (noting corrections if Earth and Moon revolve about common center).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V. Theor. V
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetas circumjoviales gravitare in Jovem, & circumsolares in Solem, & vi gravitatis suæ retrahi semper à motibus rectilineis, & in orbibus curvilineis retineri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that satellites around Jupiter gravitate toward Jupiter and planets around the Sun toward the Sun, with forces decreasing with distance similarly to gravity at Earth's surface; uses analogy with Moon-Earth and satellite eclipses and notes mutual attraction is reciprocal (Newton's third law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 (to Prop. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur gravitas datur in Planetas universos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: gravity is present in all planets; mutual attraction implies every planet attracts every other (e.g., Jupiter attracts its satellites and is attracted in turn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 (to Prop. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem, quæ Planetam unumquemque respicit, esse reciprocè ut quadratum distantiæ locorum ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States gravity toward each planet is inversely proportional to the square of distance from its center (extension of inverse-square law to planetary bodies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VI. Theor. VI
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora omnia in Planetas singulos gravitare, & pondera eorum in eundem quemvis Planetam, paribus distantiis à centro Planetæ, proportionalia esse quantitati materiæ in singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that every part of a body gravitates toward any planet and that weights (accelerative attractions) at equal distances are proportional to the quantities of matter (i.e., mass); supported by experiments comparing falling times of different materials and by arguments from satellites' regular motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 (to Prop. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc pondera corporum non pendent ab eorum formis & texturis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary arguing that weights do not depend on shape or texture: if they did, variation with form would contradict observed equality of fall times; experimental trials with pendula and different materials are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 (to Prop. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur corpora universa quæ circa Terram sunt, gravia sunt in Terram; & pondera omnium, quæ æqualiter à centro Terræ distant, sunt ut quantitates materiæ in iisdem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: all bodies near Earth are attracted by Earth and their weights at equal distances are proportional to their masses; includes thought-experiments on transforming forms and mass distribution to rule out form-dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 3 (to Prop. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Itaque Vacuum necessariò datur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues necessity of vacuum: if all spaces were filled with matter of high density, lighter bodies would not descend through it, contradicting observation; thus some vacua must exist (argument from specific gravities and descent in fluids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 4 (to Prop. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem diversi generis esse à vi magnetica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts gravity is distinct from magnetic force: magnetic attraction varies by body and can be switched on/off and decays faster than inverse square for separation, so magnetic force is of different character from universal gravitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII. Theor. VII
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem in corpora universa fieri, eamque proportionalem esse quantitati materiæ in singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that gravitational attraction occurs between all bodies and is proportional to the amounts of matter (mass) in each; argument uses composition of attractions from parts and Newton's third law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 (to Prop. VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oritur igitur & componitur gravitas in Planetam totum ex gravitate in partes singulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the total attraction of a body arises from the sum of attractions of its parts; analogy with magnetic and electric attractions composing from parts is given; notes why mutual gravitation of nearby small bodies may be imperceptible due to small magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 (to Prop. VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatio in singulas corporis particulas æquales est reciprocè ut quadratum distantiæ locorum à particulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States attraction of equal particles is inversely proportional to the square of their distances, referencing earlier propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII. Theor. VIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Globorum duorum in se mutuò gravitantium materia undique, in regionibus quæ à centris æqualiter distant, homogenea sit: erit pondus Globi alterutrius in alterum reciprocè ut quadratum distantiæ inter centra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For two spherical homogeneous bodies, the weight (attraction) of one on the other is inversely as the square of the distance between centers; Newton notes earlier doubts about exactness near surfaces but references proofs in Book I showing exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 (to Prop. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc inveniri & inter se comparari possunt pondera corporum in diversos Planetas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses orbital periods and apparent diameters to compute comparative weights on different planets and derives ratios of weights on surfaces of Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Earth under observational data (gives numerical examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 (to Prop. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur pondera corporum æqualium, in superficiebus Terræ & Planetarum, sunt fere in ratione dimidiata diametrorum apparentium è Sole visarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concludes that weights on planetary surfaces are approximately proportional to half the apparent diameters of the bodies as seen from the Sun; discusses uncertainty in Earth's apparent diameter from the Sun and implications for solar parallax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 3 (to Prop. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innotescit etiam quantitas materiæ in Planetis singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infers quantities of matter (masses) of planets from the comparative weights and distances; notes sensitivity to assumed solar parallax and gives proportional relations (e.g., relative masses of Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Earth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 4 (to Prop. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innotescunt etiam densitates Planetarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From apparent diameters and computed masses, derives planetary densities and gives numerical ratios (shows Earth much denser than Sun etc.), and comments on relation to solar heating and accommodation of materials to temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 5 (to Prop. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum autem densitates inter se fere sunt in ratione composita ex ratione distantiarum à Sole & ratione dimidiata diametrorum apparentium è Sole visarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States planetary densities approximately follow a compound ratio from distance to the Sun and half the apparent solar diameters; uses these to argue for placement of planets to receive appropriate solar heat given density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX. Theor. IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitatem pergendo à superficiebus Planetarum deorsum decrescere in ratione distantiarum à centro quam proximè.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that gravity decreases with distance from planetary surfaces approximately in the ratio of distances from the centers; exactness depends on internal density distribution (error arises from nonuniform density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X. Theor. X
rubrics_metrics.description: Motus Planetarum in Coelis diutissimè conservari posse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues planetary motions can persist for very long times because resistance of the medium (if any) is extremely small relative to planetary inertia; includes scaling of resistance with medium density and estimates showing that in rarer media resistance nearly vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XI. Theor. XI
rubrics_metrics.description: Commune centrum gravitas Terræ Solis & Planetarum omnium quiescere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the common center of gravity of Earth, Sun and all planets either rests or moves uniformly in a straight line; if it were moving, it would contradict a prior hypothesis (Hypothesis IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XII. Theor. XII
rubrics_metrics.description: Solem motu perpetuo agitari sed nunquam longe recedere à communi gravitatis centro Planetarum omnium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that although the Sun is perpetually moved by planetary attractions, it cannot recede far from the common center of gravity; gives arguments using mass ratios (e.g., Sun to Jupiter ~1100:1) and distances to locate the center near the Sun's surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. (to Prop. XII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc commune gravitatis centrum Terræ, Solis & Planetarum omnium pro centro Mundi habendum est.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concludes that the common center of gravity of Earth, Sun and planets should be taken for the center of the world; argues against the popular opinion that bodies gravitate to a fixed central point and shows the center of gravity is the appropriate resting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIII. Theor. XIII
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetæ moventur in Ellipsibus umbilicum habentibus in centro Solis, & radiis ad centrum illud ductis areas describunt temporibus proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives a priori that planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus and that radii drawn to that center sweep out areas proportional to times, noting planetary mutual actions are small and give only minor perturbations (quantifies Jupiter/Saturn perturbations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV. Theor. XIV
rubrics_metrics.description: Orbium Aphelia & Nodi quiescunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that aphelia and nodes of orbits remain fixed (quiescent) under certain assumptions; acknowledges small inequalities arise from mutual actions of planets and comets but they are negligible for present purposes (Corollaries assert fixed stars too and negligible stellar parallax).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 (to Prop. XIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quiescunt etiam Stellæ fixæ, propterea quod datas ad Aphelia Nodosque positiones servant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary: fixed stars remain practically fixed because they preserve given positions of aphelia and nodes (used to argue stars' effective immobility relative to solar system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 (to Prop. XIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideoque cum nulla sit earum parallaxis sensibilis ex Terræ motu annuo oriunda, vires earum ob immensam corporum distantiam nullos edent sensibiles effectus in regione Systematis nostri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concludes stellar gravitational effects on the solar system are negligible because stellar distances are immense and produce no sensible forces in our region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XV. Theor. XV
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire Orbium transversas diametros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides procedure: transverse diameters are taken in sesquialtera ratio of orbital periods (per Prop. XV Lib. I) and then adjusted by a ratio involving sums of masses of Sun and planet (refers to Prop. LX, Lib. I) — computational recipe rather than a statement of physical law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVI. Prob. I
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire Orbium Excentricitates & Aphelia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: find orbital eccentricities and aphelia; refers to solution provided by Prop. XVIII Lib. I (method for computing orbital elements from observed quantities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVII. Theor. XVI
rubrics_metrics.description: Planetarum motus diurnos uniformes esse, & librationem Lunæ ex ipsius motu diurno oriri.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts planets have uniform diurnal rotations and the Moon's libration arises from its diurnal rotation; refers to earlier motion laws and corollaries and explains libration in longitude and latitude from axial inclination and rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVIII. Theor. XVII
rubrics_metrics.description: Axes Planetarum dimetris quæ ad eosdem axes normaliter ducuntur minores esse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that planetary axes measured along the axis of rotation are shorter (oblateness) due to the diurnal circular motion and centrifugal effects; cites observations (Cassini, Flamsteed) and explains fluid redistribution toward the equator producing equatorial bulge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIX. Prob. II
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire proportionem axis Planetæ ad diametros eidem perpendiculares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem asking to determine the proportion of a planet's axis to its equatorial diameter; solution involves multiple computations and examples — Newton gives a calculation for Earth's oblateness from centrifugal force vs gravity, yielding numerical ratio and equatorial bulge estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XX. Prob. III
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire & inter se comparare pondera corporum in regionibus diversis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem to find and compare weights of bodies in different regions (latitudes, planetary surfaces); Newton shows weights vary reciprocally with distance from center and derives how weight increment from equator to poles relates approximately to square of sine of latitude, with numerical examples for Paris, Goree, Cayenne.
